These ten conditional hypotheses are drawn from my prior knowledge of NAS-Bench-201 rather than from running any experiments here, so none of them has been checked against benchmark data.

1. Edit: edge 3 to nor_conv_3x3. Condition: edge 5 is nor_conv_3x3. Effect is lower, because a strong conv path through node 2 already supplies capacity, so the direct edge adds less.
2. Edit: edge 5 to nor_conv_3x3. Condition: edge 3 is nor_conv_3x3. Effect is lower, from diminishing returns when the output already receives a strong conv input.
3. Edit: edge 4 to nor_conv_3x3. Condition: edge 0 is nor_conv_3x3. Effect is higher, because edge 4 only contributes when node 1 carries a learned feature, and a conv on edge 0 provides that.
4. Edit: edge 0 to nor_conv_3x3. Condition: edge 4 is nor_conv_3x3. Effect is higher, because a strong conv from node 1 to the output makes the new conv on edge 0 count.
5. Edit: edge 3 to none. Condition: edge 5 is none. Effect is lower, because removing the direct edge hurts more when there are few alternative routes to the output.
6. Edit: edge 5 to none. Condition: edge 3 is none. Effect is lower, because this is damage concentration, as with the removal of edge 3 above.
7. Edit: edge 3 to skip_connect. Condition: edge 1 is none. Effect is higher, because a skip gives the largest gradient and optimization benefit when the network otherwise has few shortcut paths.
8. Edit: edge 2 to nor_conv_1x1. Condition: edge 0 is none. Effect is lower, because edge 2 then receives no input from node 1, so the edit does almost nothing.
9. Edit: edge 1 to nor_conv_3x3. Condition: edge 3 is nor_conv_3x3. Effect is lower, from diminishing returns when a strong direct conv already exists.
10. Edit: edge 3 to nor_conv_1x1. Condition: edge 3 is currently none. Effect is higher, because replacing a removed edge is a large gain, while replacing an existing stronger op such as a 3x3 conv gains little or loses accuracy.
